questions.q: State the adjustment journal entry for outstanding wages of ₹5,000 and explain where each account appears in the final accounts.
questions.a: Correct entry: Wages A/c Dr. 5,000 → Outstanding Wages A/c 5,000. Wages expense increases by ₹5,000 in the Trading Account (debit side); Outstanding Wages appears as a current liability in the Balance Sheet. A wrong answer (e.g., debiting Outstanding Wages) reveals the student confuses the direction of the entry — they think the liability account is debited because it's "new", not understanding that expenses are debited to increase them.

questions.q: A trial balance shows Insurance Premium ₹12,000. Additional info: ₹3,000 relates to next year. A student writes the entry: Insurance A/c Dr. 3,000 → Prepaid Insurance A/c 3,000. Is this correct? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: No, it's incorrect. The correct entry is Prepaid Insurance A/c Dr. 3,000 → Insurance A/c 3,000. The student reversed the accounts because they think "prepaid is an asset so debit it" but forget that the expense must be reduced (credited) to remove the next-year portion. This reveals a mechanical memorisation of "debit asset" without understanding the dual effect: we are transferring part of an expense to an asset.

questions.q: From the following, calculate the amount of Rent to be debited to P&L and the Prepaid Rent to be shown in the Balance Sheet: Rent paid during the year ₹1,80,000 (covers 18 months from 1st Oct 2016). Accounting year ends 31st March 2017.
questions.a: Step 1: Period covered = 18 months from 1 Oct 2016 → ends 31 March 2018. Step 2: Current year = 1 Oct 2016 to 31 March 2017 = 6 months. Step 3: Monthly rent = ₹1,80,000 / 18 = ₹10,000. Step 4: Current year expense = 6 × ₹10,000 = ₹60,000 (debited to P&L). Step 5: Prepaid = ₹1,80,000 − ₹60,000 = ₹1,20,000 (current asset in Balance Sheet). A wrong answer (e.g., 12 months expense) shows the student cannot map the payment period to the accounting year.

questions.q: Compare the effect on Net Profit and Total Assets of (a) Outstanding Salary ₹10,000 and (b) Prepaid Insurance ₹10,000. Assume no other changes.
questions.a: (a) Outstanding Salary: Profit decreases by ₹10,000 (expense ↑); Total Assets unchanged (no asset created, only liability ↑). (b) Prepaid Insurance: Profit increases by ₹10,000 (expense ↓); Total Assets unchanged (one asset ↓ cash, another asset ↑ prepaid — net zero). A student who says both increase assets or both decrease profit fails to see that outstanding creates a liability, not an asset, and prepaid swaps one asset for another.

questions.q: A firm has Outstanding Rent ₹5,000 and Prepaid Rent ₹5,000. The accountant nets them off and shows zero in the Balance Sheet. Evaluate this treatment.
questions.a: Incorrect. AS 1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies) and the Companies Act require gross presentation: Outstanding Rent is a current liability; Prepaid Rent is a current asset. Netting violates the principle of separate disclosure of assets and liabilities. A student who agrees shows they confuse "net effect zero" with "correct presentation" — they don't understand that financial statements must show each item distinctly for users' decision-making.

questions.q: Create a realistic scenario (Indian context) where a business has both outstanding wages and prepaid rent. Write the adjustment entries, show the P&L and Balance Sheet extracts, and explain why both adjustments are necessary for true profit.
questions.a: Scenario: A garment shop pays ₹2,00,000 rent on 1 Jan 2017 for 12 months (year ends 31 March). March wages ₹15,000 unpaid. Entries: (1) Wages A/c Dr. 15,000 → Outstanding Wages A/c 15,000. (2) Prepaid Rent A/c Dr. 1,50,000 → Rent A/c 1,50,000. P&L: Wages ₹15,000 added; Rent ₹50,000 charged (₹2,00,000 − ₹1,50,000). Balance Sheet: Outstanding Wages ₹15,000 (liability); Prepaid Rent ₹1,50,000 (asset). Both needed: without (1), profit is overstated (wage expense missing); without (2), profit is understated (rent expense includes next year). A poor answer omits the "why" or misallocates periods.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Outstanding expenses are expenses that have been incurred during the current ______ period but remain unpaid at the end of that period; they are recorded by debiting the concerned expense account and crediting an outstanding expense liability account.
Fill in the blank: Your ______ shows you the trial balance: salaries paid ₹2,50,000 and rent paid ₹1,20,000.
What is Outstanding expenses? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Outstanding expenses are expenses that have been incurred during the current accounting period but remain unpaid at the end of that period; they are recorded by debiting the concerned expense account and crediting an outstanding expense liability account.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Outstanding expenses?
questions.a: Students often think "Outstanding expense means we haven't recorded it at all, so we debit Outstanding Expense A/c" — they treat the liability account as an expense account.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) identify outstanding and prepaid expenses from a given trial balance and additional information, (2) pass the correct adjustment journal entries for each, (3) show the treatment in the Trading and Profit & Loss Account (adding outstanding to expense, deducting prepaid from expense), and (4) present them.
